utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Now we are back to Courtroom I. Today, we are sitting in the absence of Judge Flavia Lattanzi, who is indisposed today. I hope she will recover very soon. Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's conclude your cross-examination in 40 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order to be fair to you, yesterday you mentioned Renovica. Is it the Renovica who had a moustache and who was in the State Security in the old system as well, so he's an old professional operative?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of Mile Renovica, who was the chief of the State Security Service for Vogosca and Ilijas. He did have a moustache. I don't know how long he was employed in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was he introduced by the Serbian Democratic Party after the 1990s or was he in the service before that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order to be fair to you, if this is an old cadre, then I did recall him, and you are correct. But I thought that you were thinking of a cadre of the Serbian Democratic Party, and there was no such person. All right. Can you please tell us if you know what happened on the 4th of May in Kotonje and after that in Vlahovici?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're specifically thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, did the -- were the Serbs in Kotonje attacked as a minority community, and that many of them fled to Grahoviste, and that they were captured and intercepted in Grahoviste and then later killed? That was the group that was killed later?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you put a number of questions and assertions here. Serbs in Kotonje were not a minority community, absolutely not, because there was a significant number of Serbs in Kotonje who lived there and worked there. I'm not aware that they were attacked on the 4th of May, and I'm not aware that they fled from Kotonje to Grahoviste. It wasn't logical for somebody, even if they were attacked, had a need to escape from Kotonje to Grahoviste. It would have been logical if they had a need to escape from Kotonje somewhere. Then it would have made sense to flee towards the centre of Vogosca, to that area, because the Serbs were already in power there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If they had to pass by an armed group or something, I would agree with that. But let us now look at 1D3341 in the e-court. I believe that there is a translation. This is an announcement by the Crisis Staff of the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca, and states that in relation to the arrests of nine ethnic Serbs at Grahoviste on the 3rd and 4th of May, it is again informing the public about certain details of the arrests. I would like to ask that this page not be broadcast. It states: "One day before the arrests took place, Hamdija Ackar, a well-known grocer from Kobilja Glava had arrived in Grahoviste ..." Do you know this Hamdija Ackar?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: " ... and started ensuring inhabitants that there was no reason to be afraid of Muslims. However, he advised them not to separate, and if they had any weapons, not to fire. They spoke merrily, and then immediately after he left, the -- right after he had left, Green Berets came from the direction of the Salatovic [phoen] houses, with rifles pointed at the people, and took away 11 men. They had been taken through the woods to Barice." Is this village of Barice close to Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Barice is between Kotonje and Ugorsko, and it's part of the Vogosca municipality territory. So if you're going from the direction of Kobilja Glava, you have Kobilja Glava, Hotonj, Glavica, Ugorsko, and Vogosca as a populated area.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could all parties please look at this. And then after that, I would like to look at page 2 in the Serbian. I believe that it's also page 2 in the English, and I would kindly ask that the document not be broadcast. I'm not going to be reading it out loud. Page 2 of both versions, please. You can see that it states here "Haris Trnka; Cutura, Murat," and so on. I'm not going to be reading the names, so please can everybody look at the second paragraph on this page. How is it possible that neighbours who -- no. Well, up in the previous area, it says when they had arrived in Busci, Obren Sikiras and Mile Palija were released, thanks to certain local Muslims, while the other 9 were stripped naked and taken away. And then it says that the neighbours did see and know who did that. Do you see these names?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say that in the Bosnian, but I do understand. I can see the Cyrillic writing, and I can see the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you like to read it in the English? If you cannot read it in this Bosnian that doesn't exist, perhaps you can read it in English. Perhaps it would be easier for you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you not to insult me. The language I speak is called Bosnian. I'm a Bosniak by ethnicity, I'm a Muslim by faith, and yesterday you referred to my ethnic group by its religious name. If you would like to be fair until the end, I would like you to use the official terms. I speak the Bosnian language. I understand the language that you speak. By ethnicity, I'm a Bosniak, and I'm a Muslim by faith. I don't want to be insulted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are possessing the -- laying claim on the language. It's actually the Serbian language. You called yourselves Muslims and Bosniaks, and you would be upset if you were referred to as something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, trading insults with the witness is not only wasting your time, it's wasting the whole of the Court's time. Now, please just carry on and ask specific questions relating to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree completely. I shouldn't have been caught on his hook.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, anyway, since you read in English -- you can read English, do you see these three names here, sir?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see all three of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know each of these three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that these families were mistaken and they don't know who took away their relatives?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you know what I want to say? Yesterday, you asked me, too, about this event, you put questions to me about it, and I said that in this instance, I didn't participate in any way in this incident, and that I am prepared before any court in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the world, or before an international court, to reply to questions on this incident. In this incident, I had no part in it, I had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, while the witness did offer something with respect to name recognition of some of the individuals involved, he flatly denied any involvement in the incident that's brought out in the document, Your Honours, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the incident, itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As regards the incident, Your Honour, I'm not accepting and we're not prepared to accept that it took place in any way that was depicted in this document. I also don't find the incident to be at all relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to reply, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson is going to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Well, first of all, we think that the witness's answers without the document wouldn't have that much context, and this is a situation where the document provides sufficient context for his answers that it should be admitted. And while it is true that he has denied the allegations about himself in the document, I think it would be unfortunate if the Chamber didn't receive a document simply -- that's so relevant to a witness and to their credibility simply because the witness denied parts of its contents. So I think there's sufficient elements within the witness's answer to admit the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In order to understand the context of the witness's evidence, we admit this. Give the Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1110, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3326, please. And can this document also not be broadcast, please. I don't know if we have a translation, but the date is the 12th of May. All right, we do have a translation. Can we now look at page 4, please. In the Serbian, it's at the top, in the right-hand column: "According to eye-witnesses, Serbs and Muslims arrived ..." And so on and so forth. Can you look at that, please. In the English, it's page 6, but, yes, we have it: "According to the Serbian Muslim eye-witnesses ..." And it says here -- actually, it repeats the same thing and says that they were taken to Barice and the arrest was made by -- you can see who it is. You can see, again, what it says, and then: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Vogosca will do everything in their power to exchange the nine arrested Serbs for the detainees from Svrake who participated in the armed attack on Vogosca."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with this? Do you know that these nine people were exhumed and that traces of slaughter and massacre were found on them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While giving testimony here, I heard about it here. I don't know if it was found that their throats had been cut and that they had been massacred. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not this time. This is just a news clipping, and the witness didn't confirm anything. And I think it's sufficient to have admitted 1D3341, not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I remind you -- or, actually, do you agree -- do you remember that on the 18th of April, the Green Berets, and the Muslim part of the MUP, and SDA activists from Vogosca attacked the Pretis factory on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which incident are you thinking of, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, there was one single major incident by these formations. Members of the Green Berets, the Muslim part of the MUP, and the SDA activist attacked the Pretis factory, the military factory Pretis. It was a large attack. Did that attack take place?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not saying the correct things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Enlighten us, tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With pleasure. On the 18th of April, a special unit of the Ministry of the Interior, and you refer to them as the Muslim part of the MUP. Actually, it was the special unit of the Ministry of the Interior under the command of Dragan Vikic. It's generally known that Dragan Vikic is not a Muslim. I hope you know that as well. You know very well who that man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dragan Vikic is a Croat. He was a member of the Muslim-Croat coalition; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask you not to interrupt me. It's not important to me, what Dragan Vikic is by ethnicity. In this context, it's important to know that he's not a Muslim. The unit that he commanded throughout the war was completely multi-ethnic. It had Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats, and other ethnicities. On the 18th of April, they entered the Pretis factory and they took some of the weapons that were needed for the defence of the town of Sarajevo. Thank God that they were successful, because by doing that they saved hundreds of people from your shells and from your crimes. This was a legal and legitimate action carried out by a unit of the legal Ministry of the Interior, and the weapons, in any case, belonged to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What was left of the weapons fell into your hands, and it is well known how and how often you used it, all the way until NATO bombed that particular factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know that the Yugoslav People's Army, or rather its unit that was guarding the factory, refused the warnings and the assistance offered by the Serbian side because they did not consider the Serbian side as an existing entity? They considered this factory to be the property of the JNA, and, therefore, no attack by the MUP can be considered legal if the target is a legal installation of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you are presenting erroneous facts. This factory was not guarded by any JNA unit. The factory had its own internal security service. Security officers, as they call them in English. This unit was led by Risto Bajalo. You mentioned him here. And as I said, there was no JNA unit guarding the factory. The responsibility for providing external security was under the remit of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And these security officers within the factory, under whose command were they?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the command of Risto Bajalo, a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Risto Bajalo, under whose command was he?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you the factory had its own internal security service. Therefore, Risto Bajalo was an employee of the factory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3327.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, was this part of Pretis factory a military plant?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at the column on the left, paragraph 3. It says: "Members of the Green Berets and the so-called BH MUP carried out an armed attack on the Unis factories in Vogosca, which resulted in the first casualty. On that occasion, some of the Pretis special-purposes, industry-produced products and a large number of the cars were looted and stolen. This prompted the Serbs to take power in the municipality, and all of this affected and resulted in the suspension of the production." Is this the event that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have already put forth a number of assertions that are absolutely untrue. This event could not possibly be the last straw that induced the Serbian Crisis Staff to take power in Vogosca, because they had already had power in Vogosca and did what they wanted. I'm telling you again, that was a legal police operation. There were no Green Berets, no activists, no hoards, as you often call them in your statements, took part in this operation. Therefore, we are talking about a legal police operation carried out by the legal forces of the BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the victims were also legal?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were -- what kind of casualties are you talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many Green Berets were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This operation was carried out so superbly that not a single member of the police force, which you call Green Beret, was wounded. You probably have wrong information provided to you by your people from Vogosca. Nobody was killed, and none of the Pretis employees were among the casualties. There were only casualties the following day. The first operation was carried out during the night; whereas, the next day there are casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, look at this: "They burst into it on the 17th of April, and then they came back on the 18th of April to capture the factory, which caused tremendous casualties." Do not qualify my question. Does it say here that the Crisis Staff took power at that point, and that was on the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely don't understand what you are trying to say. You have cited a number of things that don't hold water, and I don't understand them. You are completely lost in asking questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say that on the 13th of May, 1992, that this event was the cause for the Serbs to take power?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not interested at all in reading any pamphlet printed by the SDS. This is a Chetnik and a Greater Serbian pamphlet full of lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a municipal bulletin, not a pamphlet.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it a joint municipality or just a Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Only the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So now you expect me to accept the statements of Chetnik provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you see, sir, why you have been branded as a dangerous extremist.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to answer this question. Mr. Accused, I am a Muslim, and I will remain a Muslim forever. You are not a relevant person -- you're absolutely not a relevant person, particularly in the position that you are in, to judge whether I am an extremist or not. This is up to you. I am telling the truth here, and I refuse to be insulted. I cannot be anything else but a Muslim. However, your blind hate of the Muslims is your problem; it's not my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see what is written here about the 3rd of May, saying that Green Berets from Kobilja Glava, together with HOS, attacked Blagovac? Was Blagovac and part of Hotonj, where Serbs lived, attacked as well as the central part of Vogosca? Did that take place on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some combat operation. I don't know which operation you're having in mind. I don't know whether there was one on the 3rd of May, but there were no HOS members or Green Berets taking part in these operations where police and the regular Territorial Defence, which was later renamed Army of BH. Of course, you find it difficult to say the name of BH Army because they have caused so much trouble for you. And, of course, we are talking about regular MUP police forces. But I do understand your need to distort the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the BH Army exist on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a regular and a lawful Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which would later grow into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, what was the basis for this regular, whatever you wish to call it, force, to attack Kotonje, the Serbian village of Blagovac, Krivoglavci, and the central parts of Vogosca? What was the reason for that attack?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the TO and the police did not attack the Serbian village of Blagovac, as you say, although in this village, the Serbs were a dominant community. But there were also Bosniaks and Albanians living there as well. Now, from these positions -- positions from Krivoglavci, from Blagovac, from the central parts, there were shells fired on a daily basis. What do you expect them to do? Should they have been sitting and not responding to fire? People were being killed by shells, by snipers. The power -- the power was cut, the water supply was cut. Did you expect us to sit quietly and just look at it without doing anything? You, as a peacemaker, wanted to ethnically cleanse Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please refrain from these patterns. Were you fired at from Vogosca and all these parts before the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask you again not to interrupt me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are wasting my time. Please answer my questions. Don't ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please calm down. And you don't have much time, Mr. Karadzic. Just ask the questions one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question is clear. Are you saying that -- as you say, the fact that fire was being opened, did that happen before the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had started firing before the 7th of January, 1992, from artillery guns, from sniper rifles. You were using the whole arsenal of weapons that you had at your disposal. Are you trying to tell me that that is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are going to ask the OTP to corroborate your statement with appropriate documents. Can we have this document tendered into evidence, because it was a contemporaneous document drafted at the time of the event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you put your question to the witness based upon the viewpoint of this article, and the witness answered clearly to the questions, so we don't need -- we don't need this article to understand the context of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 1D3346. This is news from Bosnia, published by the Sandzak News Forum, which is a Muslim forum based in Sandzak, in Serbia, and it says here: "On the night between the 17th and 18th of April, special MUP units, based on the previous co-operation, established contacts with the most responsible people from Vogosca and demanded support for carrying out an operation in order to take out equipment and materiel from the Vogosca Pretis factory and take them away from TO Vogosca." It says here that a number of Patriotic League were involved in this. Then it says that from Stari Grad municipality, units were dispatched. And towards the bottom, it says part of the unit TO Novi Grad, led by the late Safet Hadzic - and later on a street was named after him - Safet Hadzic, unfortunately, with his van came to the unit's main gate, where from the forest and the bunker across, they were faced with Chetnik bursts of fire from machine-guns. Do you agree that a number of people were killed on that occasion and that Safet Hadzic was amongst them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Witness: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It would have been useful to have been notified about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree and I apologise, but this is the result of the witness's rebuttal of things that are generally known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is something from one's blog. Yes, in any event, can you answer the question, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I can, Your Honours. This was taken off a private Internet provider. Anyone can have their blog on the Internet, and they can put on it whatever they please. I absolutely don't want to comment what is written here, because a huge number of things stated here are not true. It's your problem, if you had been using this for your propaganda purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a Muslim blog, sir?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I browsed the Internet very often, and I don't care whether any blog is Muslim, Croatian, Australian, Israeli, or whatever. I don't view them in that way. I don't know if it is Muslim. Objectively speaking, it could have been created by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbs, in that case, would have called it "Raska." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. For me, Sandzak is Sandzak, and you may call it what you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you dispute that Safet Hadzic, a hero after whom a street was named, was killed on the night between the 17th and 18th on the attack on Pretis?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Safet Hadzic was killed one day after the operation carried out by the MUP special unit. I haven't finished. So the special unit carried out an attack during the night, and before dawn they left the premises of the factory. Safet Hadzic, however, was killed sometime around noon on the following day.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this blog admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have no basis, Mr. Karadzic, to admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we now have 1D3340, and can it please not be broadcast. This is a document that was retrieved from the archives, and it was created from the 1993/1994 section. We still don't have a translation. I'm going to read it. Archive document. The year is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is another document which was not notified?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really sorry, but this pace is really killing me, and it is affecting our ability to present evidence, and it can also jeopardise our health. Now, I am going to present this to everyone concerned. This is an archived document kept in the archives, and this document was created in 1993 and 1994. Can we please have page 4. Do not broadcast this. Here, listed are the activities, the crimes, and the mistreatment, and the names of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, if you'll look on the column on the left, paragraph 3, "Nijaz Grebovac" and the others, look at these names. Do you see that according to these archived documents, all these people took part in organised taking away of the Serbs to Kosevo, where they were executed? They also carried out preparations for combat and provided arms to the Muslims? Can you see these five names here?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of these five names that we see here, only two are people from Kobilja Glava. So that is incorrect, for starters. I have already denied participation in what you are trying to impose on all of us here now, so this doesn't really mean anything to me, that my name is contained in your archives. As a matter of fact, I am pleased that that is the case, because it means how worthy I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at these names. Where it says, at the very bottom, that during lunch, they killed the Ristovic family sometime in the summer of 1992. Is it true that the Ristovic family was found having lunch at home and then they were killed, all of them? Just say that, don't be afraid.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't you worry about me. I'm not afraid. It is true that the Ristovic family was killed. Nobody is denying that, and don't you worry about me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about these starting with the letters "Zh" onwards?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know each and every one of them because they live there -- they lived there, rather, at Kobilja Glava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's no secret.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted, or marked for identification before it's translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what's the provenance of the document? "An archival document" means absolutely nothing to us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain? The Army of Republika Srpska and the ministry were abolished, but all of this material has been archived, and that was done then in 1993 and 1994. That's the date of the document, and these complete archives were established. And the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska no longer exists, but the archives remained within the joint documentation. I'm afraid that you have been notified of this document, that the Prosecution had been notified that this document would crop up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, have you heard of a person by the name of Milorad Bukva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never heard of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We mark it for identification, but only for the purpose of understanding the context of the witness, because this was put to the witness. He identified some names and some incidents, not beyond any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We just -- I don't know what the document is at all. That's the basis of my question, and I'm still no clearer on what the document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Really? I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something before you reach your decision? These are archived documents, and they have become part of the archives of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And notice was provided yesterday that I would be using this document during the cross-examination. These are voluminous archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At this moment, we are not satisfied with the foundation of this document, Mr. Karadzic. And some parts of this document was recognised by the witness, and I think it's sufficient by this. At this moment, we would not admit this document. You have five minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly request a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you sure that these paramilitaries existed in your day in Vogosca, these White Eagles and whatever, and how did you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, specifically, Mr. Accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned in different statements and during the examination-in-chief that there were different paramilitary groups there, that the White Eagles and Seselj's men were there, and that you recognised them by the white eagles that they wore?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a generally-known thing that Seselj's soldiers, the White Eagles, were in Vogosca. They were put up at the Park Hotel. Any child in Vogosca knew that. Any inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina knew that. It is a generally-known fact that they took part in military operations, and their leader, Seselj - do not interrupt me, I haven't finished - said in public several times that that was the case, and he boasted about the participation of his soldiers in the fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You've already said that. Up until November -- oh, I'm sure that we will probably have to move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I'd like to apologise and correct myself. I'm sorry, we don't need to be in private session for this, but I thought I'd better do it sooner, rather than later. With respect to the last document, I was ill-informed as to the notification, and we misunderstood the notification e-mail, and I very much wanted to make my apologies to everyone in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's paragraph 30 of your amalgamated statement, where it says: [In English] "First, I would like to explain that at this meeting, there was also the chief of the Security Services Centre present ..." [Interpretation] And so on: [In English] "Probably they planned that Maksimovic would be present at the meeting." [Interpretation] Who is "they," who is the "they"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're trying to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, we'll leave that aside. We don't have enough time. Do you have the amalgamated statement there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we up-load his amalgamated statement, para 30, around the region of page 9. I take it there's no B/C/S version of his amalgamated statements. He's referring to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this part here? There was a meeting. Koprivica mentioned Momo. Then Tintor was there. And then Tintor's answer that Momo was in the Assembly. So you are saying here that -- well, you were probably interpreting some intercepted conversation. Krajisnik was president of the Assembly, while Momo Mandic was not a member of the Assembly and wouldn't have any reason to be there: [In English] "That is why I am sure Krajisnik is referred to here. I am certain that Koprivica had contacted Krajisnik to let him know about the problem, and that he asked for the instructions on how to act." [Interpretation] Did you know that? Are you firmly convinced that it is so? Do you have any proof that he called him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I knew, because Koprivica on several occasions said that to me, as far as this particular problem was concerned as well, that he would not take a single step without consulting Momo Krajisnik. So I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you draw the following conclusion: "That means that Krajisnik ..." [In English] " ... had the authority to give an order to be implemented through Koprivica and Tintor." [Interpretation] Is this something that you drafted, or did somebody ask you to interpret what Krajisnik could do and what that would mean?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you're putting an unclear question to me. I already gave a specific answer. On several occasions, Rajko Koprivica told me, even about this problem, that he would not make any moves without first consulting Momcilo Krajisnik, and you know that is so too. So there's no dilemma there. I don't know what the formulation is in the Bosnian language and how that has been translated to you into the Serbian, and then into the English in turn. And the conclusion that you draw from all of that, that is quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you: You're drawing the conclusion that this means that Krajisnik -- why didn't you write that down, that Koprivica informed you that in this case, he called Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't write this. I was speaking. I was telling the investigators, and they were writing it down. I don't know how they understood it in the English. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, I must say something here in order to be fair to you and to the OTP and to the transcript. The authors of these amalgamated statements are not witnesses. It's evident that the witness has now said that he didn't write this.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, I don't expect you to direct me. I signed this statement. It was read back to me in the English and in the Bosnian. Therefore, you cannot -- you cannot, and it does not stand as a fact -- or the allegation doesn't stand that somebody chose these words for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, who selected the words, the information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I spoke in the Bosnian. I'm not an expert in English. I don't know how the interpreter translated it. I don't know that, but I know what I said in the Bosnian. I know -- I hope you understand the Bosnian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now ask you, please, to allow me to address the Chamber. What is of concern to the Defence is the piling up of cliches and different things from one amalgamated statement to the next. This is causing the Defence to expend a lot of resources and time on that. This is not something that the witnesses have said. This is something that is created by the OTP. I do not want to insult or attack anyone, but I want to put it to the Chamber that, as far as we're concerned, it's confusing, coming from our legal system, it presents a burden, because an investigating judge would not allow such things to be part of the statement unless he could see that it was corroborated or not. These amalgamated statements are full of general statements, political cliches, and it is my only hope that this Trial Chamber, as the Chamber of Judges, professionals, without a jury, will be able to establish what's what. But I would really like to ask the Trial Chamber to ask the OTP to stop burdening us with quantity, rather than quality, at the expense of quality. The Defence is snowed under a vast number of statements that are uncorroborated and which would not be acceptable in our legal system. Thank you, I am finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's hope the Judges will be able to sift the wheat from the chaff. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: (redacted), I'd like to ask you a couple of additional questions --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I need a redaction, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions based on your testimony of the last couple of days; to begin with, some evidence that you gave yesterday. At page 12492, line 10, referring to September 1991, you said that: "The Crisis Staff at Vogosca was established at the time I mentioned." You also said: "I heard from Serbs who were in -- I heard that from Serbs who were in official positions and didn't conceal that either." Could you tell us who you heard this from, then, and what did they say?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, the first information I got about that was from Borislav Maksimovic, and he said that, in any case, he had to listen to and do what the Crisis -- Serbian Crisis Staff decided. In a broader context, Koprivica even mentioned that, because they felt so secure and safe that they did not conceal the existence of the Serbian Crisis Staff, nor did they feel that there was a need to conceal something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've just said, in answer to my question, that you -- as to who you heard of the existence of the Crisis Staff from, you've just named Rajko Koprivica and Borislav Maksimovic. Is there any other Serb in official positions that you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Svetozar Stanic was there, who was a pretty open and quite fair man. There was Slavko Jovanovic, who was the former president of the Municipal Assembly. I was on relatively good terms with him, we communicated well. I frequently spoke with Tintor as well. He would introduce himself as the deputy president of the Serbian Democratic Party, and as a representative of all the Serbs in Vogosca, and as a member of the Serbian Crisis Staff, a person who is responsible for everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just to go further: At page 12515, lines 11 to 14, in answer to a question from Dr. Karadzic, you said that you heard from specific Serbs, who communicated with you, that the Serbs had established a territorial defence since September in Vogosca. You asked Dr. Karadzic: "Do you want me to give you the name?" And Dr. Karadzic replied: "No, no." Could you give us the name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, these are the same people that I already mentioned. But the first time I received this information was from Jovo Baranovic [phoen], who was the commander of the joint TO staff, practically. But more or less all the people that I mentioned already confirmed and spoke about that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I've been asked by my colleagues, the interpreters, if you could speak more directly into the microphone. They would be able to hear you better and be able to interpret you a bit more effectively. Now, further in your evidence of yesterday, in the discussion of the replacement of Zeljko Skrbic, which was at pages 12539 to 12540, at page 12540 you said to Dr. Karadzic: "If you allow me, I can explain to the Trial Chamber the reasons why the replacement took place." And Dr. Karadzic said: "We'll get to that." I wonder if you can explain, briefly, the reasons why the replacement of Zeljko Skrbic took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, having a look at the witness's answer, although the question didn't call for private session, I think the answer might well have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Further, at page 12549, line 10, you were asked yesterday: "Please, could you tell us against whom the president of Vogosca municipality wanted to mobilise the TO in September 1991?" And as part of your response, you said: "The situation in the municipality was already such that the existing police forces were unable to keep law and order, and it was necessary to mobilise the TO so that they could assist in improving the situation in the municipality." You referred also, at page 12571, line 15, to valid reasons to muster the TO units. And I'd like to ask you if you could tell us what, in September 1991, was the situation in Vogosca that led to the attempt to mobilise the Territorial Defence. And, please, in your answer, if you feel your answer would lead you to divulge your identity, feel free to ask for private session.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can move into private session right away, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The special police unit carried out its action during the night and, at dawn, left the Pretis compound. So the police action ended with that. There were no casualties on any side during the police action. No one was wounded, no one was killed. The police carried out their action brilliantly, in a professional way. The following way, Safet Hadzic's group - these were members of the Territorial Defence from Novi Grad - went to the Pretis factory to take weapons from there. The Pretis factory has two gates. One is called the main gate, and the second gate is called the industrial gate. The special units entered the factory through the industrial gate because it is closer from the Kobilja Glava direction. However, Safet Hadzic and his TO group from Novi Grad were not aware of this fact, and instead of entering the Pretis factory through the industrial gate, they tried to enter through the main gate. At the main gate, they were intercepted by members of the Serbian TO. And as soon as they left their vehicles, came to the main gate, these people opened fire. Safet Hadzic was killed at that time, and I don't know how many other members of the TO from Novi Grad; maybe four or five of them. Six or seven people were wounded. This is the truth, this is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have anything further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Witness. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for listening to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey back home. Please wait until we draw the curtain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wait for a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the time. We take a break for half an hour. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just very quickly, Your Honour. In the interests of overall efficiency and decorum, we try to be sparing about rising in response to comments by the accused, but in this instance -- so in this instance, let me simply say that with respect to the comments about amalgamated statements, we reject them as virtually wholly inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. While we maybe have a few minutes before we take a break, if I can address that issue. This is something that has cropped up regularly by Dr. Karadzic in our discussions, and I know he's brought this to the attention of the Chamber on several occasions, and I remember that Judge Morrison suggested that he consider addressing this issue in writing. And I just want to explain to the Chamber that basically what Dr. Karadzic asks me on many occasions, and to which I have always given him the same answer, is, What is the effect of these amalgamated statements, including many generalisations that appear in those statements? And I've told him that under Rule 92 ter, everything in an amalgamated statement is evidence as if the witness uttered those words in the courtroom, and that to the extent that he wants to challenge that evidence, he has to do so during his cross-examination. And that advice is not something that Dr. Karadzic likes to hear, because he doesn't feel he has enough time to deal with all of those matters in his cross-examination, and that's the source of the frustration that he has, that he regularly expresses to the Chamber. So I wanted to explain that. And if my advice is erroneous, then I apologise, but I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson, I don't think your advice is erroneous. Inevitably, one thing that concerns the Judges - I'm speaking, but I think I speak for my colleagues as well - is the huge amount of evidence that's coming before the Court, and, inevitably, some of it is of more probative value than others. Some of it may turn out to be of no probative value at all. But a striving by all parties to reduce the burden of evidence is going to do three things: It's going to concentrate the Court on the issues; it's going to reduce the time that the whole trial takes; and it's going to make the monumental task of writing a judgement in this case more concise and, frankly, easier. Those are all self-evident points, I suspect, but they are ones that the Judges would certainly like all parties to bear at the forefront of their thinking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if the evidence-in-chief is led live, one cannot deal with every aspect of the evidence-in-chief. Let's concentrate on important issues, and then believe in the Judges' -- professional Judges' ability. We'll adjourn for half an hour. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Muracevic. If you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Muracevic. Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Eset Muracevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As we've discussed, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing, so we first need to deal with the formalities associated with that submission. It's right, isn't it, that you've provided a number of statements generally to the Bosnian authorities, and also statements in relation to a number of suspects?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've also provided a number of statements to members of the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've also had an opportunity to review a statement which has consolidated relevant information from these prior statements into one amalgamated witness statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have 65 ter 90228 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, is this the statement that you reviewed? Do you recognise your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the statement that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you initialled each page and signed the last page; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you confirm that the statement is accurate?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the same matters contained within that statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would provide the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter number 90228, the statement of the witness, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P2361.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave, I'll now read a summary of the witness's written evidence. Prior to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the witness worked for many years as the secretary of the local commune of Svrake, in the Vogosca municipality. The witness describes events from the multi-party elections and changes that were felt in the village from that point on. At the beginning of 1992, check-points were established on all main roads. In early March 1992, Muslim-owned houses came under infantry fire and another set on fire. Barricades were established in the Svrake area. The witness describes the arming of the local Serb population by the JNA and others. Weapons from the Pretis factory in Vogosca were taken to the Semizovac military barracks, from where the local Bosnian Serb population collected automatic rifles and ammunition. At the beginning of May 1992, the village of Svrake was attacked by SDS paramilitary formations, houses destroyed, and the village plundered. On the 4th of May, 1992, when a convoy of around 600 villagers attempted to escape to the Bosnian-controlled territory of Breza, the last group of 430 villagers were stopped by police and soldiers and taken to the military barracks in Semizovac. From May until December 1992, the witness was detained in a number of different facilities under the control of the Bosnian Serb authorities. He was first detained in a facility known as the bunker, which was nearby to the local restaurant Kontiki, otherwise known as Kod Sonja. While he was held at the bunker, he was taken to another facility for one night, known as Naka's garage, where a large number of local non-Serb population were being held. Around 11 August 1992, he and other detainees were transferred from the bunker to a detention facility known as Planjo's house. The witness describes how the detainees were interrogated, beaten, abused, and threatened with death by the guards, interrogators, and various other groups, including Seselj's men, who would enter the bunker and Planjo's house. Branko Vlaco, the head of the detention facilities in Vogosca, was regularly present when the detainees were subjected to the abuse. The witness describes the conditions at the bunker. The detainees received little food, slept on cold, wet floors, and did not receive medical treatment. A number of detainees were taken from the bunker for exchange and never seen again. On a number of occasions, the witness and other detainees were taken from the bunker and Planjo's house for forced labour to the front-lines, where they were also used as human shields. A number of detainees were killed and injured doing this forced labour and being used as human shields. Bodies of those killed while forced -- doing forced labour were brought back to Planjo's house and buried by other detainees in the local cemetery. The witness describes a visit in August 1992 to Planjo's house by Momcilo Mandic and a journalist from Serb Radio/TV in Pale. Mandic told the detainees that there was no need for them to be exchanged because they were already at their homes. On the 5th of December, 1992, the witness was taken from Planjo's house to the front-line and used as a human shield, and while at the front-line, he managed to escape to Bosnian-held territory. After his escape, the witness resided in Sarajevo. He describes the terror inflicted on the population, the civilian population, by the shelling and sniping by the Bosnian Serb forces, and relates specific instances of shelling of the city between 1993 and 1995, when he was wounded as a result of the shelling. In 1996, after re-integration, the witness found a number of documents in the Vogosca municipality building and provided those documents to a number of Bosnian agencies and also to the ICTY. He provides information relating to some of these documents and also additional documents shown to him. Your Honour, that completes the summary of the witness's written evidence. I have a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, as secretary of the Local Commune of Svrake, briefly, what were your duties in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: As the Local Commune secretary, I was involved in technical issues relating to the organisation of life at the level of the Local Commune. Around 1200 people lived in my village, predominantly of Muslim ethnicity; i.e., around 1.036. There were only 170 Serbs, whereas the remaining population was composed of members from other communities, such as Croats, Yugoslavs, and those who declared themselves as the others. Before the war, my village was one of the best-known villages where good inter-ethnic relations prevailed. Therefore, there was no indication before the war of what happened later in 1992 and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to what you describe in paragraph 69 to 84 of your statement, and that is how you and other detainees were taken for forced labour and used as human shields. Can you first briefly describe for the Chamber what you had to physically do when you were taken for forced labour?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: The taking of the detainees to perform certain labour jobs from their place of detention was done under Branko Vlaco's authorisation, who was the warden of the prison. He, in a certain way, gave his approval for the detainees to be taken out. The detainees were forced to carry out various jobs, mainly on the front-lines, which included the digging of trenches, communication trenches, and other fortification features. Such jobs carried out on the front-lines actually took part along the lines of separation between the Serbian Army and the BH Army. The majority of the detainees who carried out these jobs was virtually exposed to fire from both sides. Many of the people who went to perform this labour never returned. Some of them were killed and buried at the local cemeteries either in Svrake or in the vicinity of the detention facility. Naturally, there were some jobs that were requested by the local population, which involved working the fields. Then other units made similar requests, such as the Rajlovac Brigade, Serbian Brigade. Then there were jobs relating to the Ilijas Police Station, et cetera. For the most parts, all these jobs were performed on the front-lines, where the detainees were exposed to fire from both sides. Quite a few of them, as I said, were killed while doing labour. Many were seriously wounded, and some of those seriously wounded did not receive proper medical assistance, which caused the injuries to heal in a very complicated way and it took a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, if any, psychological -- what was any psychological impact on you from -- as a result of you being used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, the very knowledge that you are between two fires enhances your fear of what might happen. I, myself, was injured once when I did the labour and I did not receive proper medical assistance, and I had complications in my left hand all through the end of my detention. Before the war, I was able to play guitar, but due to the badly-treated wound, I am not able to do that any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you actually went to work on the front-lines, what did you actually have to do?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Typically, we were digging trenches on the front-lines. On several occasions when I was there, I was involved in the digging of trenches, covering of the trenches. And once, before I escaped, I had a feeling that they were preparing us to put us forth as a human shield, because we were digging along the separation line facing Rajlovac and Zuc. All this work mainly involved the digging of trenches, carrying of ammunition and heavy weaponry, and providing their lines with materiel, whether it be ammunition or the like.

utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we can deal with the last one first. If I can have 65 ter number 14382.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, this is a request from the SJB Ilijas to the manager of the Vogosca Prison for 10 prisoners to carry out tasks for the SJB Ilijas on 12th-13th September 1992. You stated in your statement that you don't recall the names of any detainees who had to perform tasks for the SJB Ilijas, but did detainees have to undertake tasks for the SJB Ilijas, even though you are not able to recall the names of any persons that had to do that?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: They did have to work for them, because many teams came to get prisoners to do some work; inter alia, the representatives of the Police Station Ilijas. That is to say that this is just one of the documents that shows that the police station in Ilijas took inmates from the camp to do some work there. I don't know what kind of work they did for them, but the assumption is, in view of the date when this was happening, it probably had something to do with certain combat activities in the area of Ilijas, towards Ravno Nabosce [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P2386.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter number 14378 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, this is a request from the chief of the SJB Vogosca to the manager of the Vogosca Prison for eight workers (prisoners) to carry out tasks for the SJB Vogosca, dated the 1st of September, 1992. In your statement, at paragraph 88, you said that you can't recall the names of any detainees who had to perform work for the SJB Vogosca, but the same question again. Are you aware of people being taken from the detention facilities to undertake work at the Vogosca SJB, even though you're not aware of the names of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I did know that representatives of the Serb police from Vogosca took inmates away to do some work for them. As a matter of fact, during one period of time, I, myself, was taken away by them, by the representatives of this police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's contained in paragraph 34 of your amalgamated witness statement, for the Chamber and the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, the other two, Your Honour, the two telegrams dated the 6th and 10th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In order to take the witness to the first one, dated the 6th of August, I need to bring up two other documents first. If I could have Exhibit P01606. Actually, Your Honour, I don't think the witness is going to be able to go further than what's already in the statement, and I think that we could put these -- submit these documents by way of a Bar Table -- part of a Bar Table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not tendering now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Muracevic, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Radovan Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just before we do that, I just want to note for the record that the Prosecution disclosed to us the fact that this witness had testified in proceedings in Bosnia, for which we don't have his testimony yet. We're hoping to receive that at some point, and those are proceedings involving Momcilo Mandic, Mladen Milanovic, Sretko Damjanovic, and Borislav Herak. So it's my understanding he testified in trials of each of those persons, and we don't have the transcripts or the recordings of those. I just want to make a note of that. Then if it becomes necessary to ask for any relief, we'll do that in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Muracevic.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to your statements, you worked in Svrake, as secretary of the Local Commune, from 1981 until 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you, and remind myself, to take -- to make small pauses so that the interpreters can actually interpret what we are saying. Am I right when I say that before the system changed after the elections in 1990, you worked as the secretary of the Local Commune?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the time, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm pausing for the interpreters, just so that it doesn't puzzle you in any way. Did you then go on as a member of the party that was the successor of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1990, as a member of the League of Communists, I held the position of the secretary of the Municipal Conference of the Socialist Alliance of the Working People in Vogosca. After that, I was -- I became a member of the organisation that was called the Alliance of the Reformist Forces. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was headed by Nenad Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of your statements, it says "SDP," so I thought --

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the League of Communists. You know how that transformation went. The SDP was -- well, I mean, I don't know how to put this. I was a member of the League of Communists, and it was later transformed into the SDP. But just before the outbreak of the conflict, I was a member of the Alliance Of the Reformist Forces, headed by Mr. Nenad Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can also follow the transcript, and when the transcript stops, that means that the interpreters managed to interpret what we were saying. Am I right if I say that in view of those 11 or 12 years, as secretary of this local commune, you were one of the prominent citizens in your village?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can call it prominent. But as a man who carried out this technical work for the Local Commune, I was a person who everybody knew, and, in a way, I was involved in the organisation of life in the territory of the Local Commune. I was carrying out different activities related to the functioning of a village; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you note the formation of the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ before the elections in 1992 in your village?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I did note the formation of the SDS party and the SDA party in my village. Other than the political parties that were active before - I'm thinking of the League of Communists and the Socialist Alliance - there were no other options before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There weren't too many Croats there, so you didn't have the HDZ there, did you?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us who represented the SDA? Who were in the party? Who was the SDA membership in your village?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: It was mostly the local population of Muslim ethnicity, no one in particular who was prominent in that party. It was mostly the local inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the more prominent Muslims stayed faithful to the left-oriented parties, the SDP and the reformist parties, or did any of them cross over to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that many people crossed over into the SDA and the SDS, although a number of people who were in these parties did transfer to the SDS and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your consolidated statement, paragraph 3, you said that the ethnic structure of the population was 1.240 total in the village of Svrake; around 1.030 Bosniaks, 170 Serbs, 2 Croats, and 21 who declared themselves as Yugoslavs, and 18 persons -- actually, 18 per cent of other ethnicities. Who are these others? What did you think of?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Mostly the Roma, Albanians, and some others who declared themselves as others and did not declare themselves as belonging to the ethnic group that they belonged to. This is according to the ethnic -- to the census of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they did not declare themselves as being as any of the three constituent peoples, Serbs, Croats, or Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that there were fewer Serbs than these others? There was about 16 or 17 per cent of Serbs, and the others, there was 18 per cent of them?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: There were just 170 Serbs. So when you make that comparison, that's what it comes to, approximately, although the others, who declared themselves as others and as Yugoslavs, there were also Bosniaks and Serbs who did not declare themselves according to the ethnic definition or orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure if we were talking about persons or percentages.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I think it's persons, individuals, not percentages. 170 persons of Serbian ethnicity lived in my local community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that amounted to 17 per cent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I never made that calculation, but I assume that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, this was a predominantly Muslim village, not to say exclusively Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, the consolidated statement, in paragraph 4 you say -- I will have to read in English because we don't have a Serbian version: [In English] "The residents of Serb ethnicity started visiting neighbouring Serb villages more often, such as Semizovac, Krivoglavci, Paljevo Brdo. This was during 1991 and more often during the first months of 1992. It usually happened during the night, and during the day they would return to their homes to feed the cattle. Since I was secretary of the Local Commune, we organised our men of Bosniak ethnicity to look after Serb houses so that there would not be any robberies." [Interpretation] You did receive the translation. Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Trial Chamber and the participants why the Serbs spent nights in Serbian villages and not in Svrake, in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1991, at your rallies devoted to organising the plebiscite of the Serbian people, you had the habit of announcing the following: that in the municipalities and areas that would be under the control of the Serbs, you would ban the sale of properties to Muslims, you would ban the construction of houses for Muslims in territories that are under your control, and that any Muslim foundations that are built will be blown up. This you had the habit of stating at your public rallies before the plebiscite of the Serbian people. Sometime in late 1991, you publicly threatened, from the Assembly platform, that the Bosniak people would disappear if a conflict were to break out. Perhaps all of that had an effect on the local people who had some kind of instructions from representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party that we were not aware of. And as good neighbours, a place where inter-ethnic relations were good, it was strange to us why, from time to time in 1991, they were more often going to Krivoglavci, going to Paljevo, where some of them had weekend homes before. So, in a way, we were afraid that some local criminals, perhaps, could rob one of their houses. We were afraid that there would be an incident, and we were also afraid that the Serbian population was trying to bring about an incident. I must say that in 1991 or early 1992, the majority population of the Svrake Local Commune, which comprised of Muslims, did not cause a single incident that would cause such behaviour on their part. There wasn't even a single incident involving robbery of their property or anybody threatening anybody's security. I think that the fact that they kept leaving the settlements was pursuant to directions of the Serbian Democratic Party, either the local branch, the local branch that had links with the municipal organisation, which, in turn, was linked to the republican organisation under you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you trying to say that the Serbian people were so obedient that they would go to sleep and spend the night in discomfort upon recommendation of the Serbian Democratic Party? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: There was no other reason. There was no other reason. The Muslim population did not give any single cause for something like that. They had to have been listening to somebody. They didn't leave their houses because somebody was telling them to leave or driving them out. Even in conversations with them, we kept asking them not to go, but they wouldn't listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Muracevic, where did you hear that I said publicly that Muslims will not be able to build houses and settlements in Serbian territory and that foundations would be blown up? Where did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: In documents -- there is an audio-recording of such a statement. I don't have it with me. There is an audio-recording of a statement of yours, where you say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you studied those audio-recordings and documents of my speeches at the meetings of my party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Later, there was an opportunity to hear and to read all sorts of things, as they say; of course, not prior to the conflict, but after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-hah. And somebody showed you that after the war. Who was it that showed that to you?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to read that in a gazette or a bulletin of the State Commission for Investigation of War Crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-hah. So then we have to take into account that what you are saying, you are not saying based on your own experience or what you went through in the field, but based on your experiences while studying documents about war crimes, as compiled by the state; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I didn't have the opportunity to hear these transcripts and read them. I had the opportunity to read that after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
