utterances.text: And after you read that, can you please tell us, is it correct that I conveyed, at a party Planum, what I told Mr. Izetbegovic in response to his idea to move in four million Muslims from Turkey, and that I told him, Yes, you can do that, but not to Serbian areas. You are not going to artificially alter the ethnic compositions. Such settlements will not be set up in the Serbian areas. I am interpreting what I told privately to Izetbegovic, and I stated that at a closed meeting. And you say that I said that. Is it the way I said it?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's your right to say whatever you will, but what you are saying is something that I don't know. What I do know are the results of what you, together with the local authorities and the local SDS in my local community in my municipality, what you did. For example, in the territory under the control of the Serbs in the beginning of 1992, which is meaning that in a year -- in a territory controlled by Serbian forces from Vogosca, 13.127 citizens were deported, over 11.000 of whom were Bosniaks. This was in the territories that were under your control from May 1992 until mid-June 1992 [as interpreted], when the local Serbian authorities in Vogosca municipality made some kind of census. You expelled 13.127 non-Serb inhabitants, including over 11.000 Bosniaks. If this is what you were talking about with Mr. Izetbegovic privately, or reached some kind of agreement about something, then all right. But I am aware of what was happening in the territory that was under your control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will wait, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I think that there may have been an interpretation mistake. Page 71, line 1, "until mid-June 1992." Mr. Karadzic may like to clarify with the witness whether he means 1992 or 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I cannot see page 71. Something has stopped here on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The public, common computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah-hah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say here at the beginning of this page that the Serbian authorities, up until mid-June 1992, expelled 11.000 -- actually, 13.127 people?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I made an error. I'm talking about June 1993. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, sir, are you saying this as someone that you, yourself, saw, or are you talking about it based on what you read in the material given to you by the State Commission for Investigation of War Crimes?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm speaking partly from personal experience, because 1.036 Bosniaks from my village in that period left. None of them stayed. None of the Bosniaks stayed behind in Tihovici, either, which was predominantly populated by ethnic Muslims. So this is information partially obtained during the war. According to the documents, upon the integration of Vogosca as part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation, dealing with the Vogosca municipality, a report by the Census Commission indicates how many citizens there were in 1993 in territory controlled by Serbian forces. So from May 1992 until this census in June 1993, 13.127 non-Serb citizens were deported, expelled, placed into camps from the territory under your control. This included more than 11.000 Bosniaks, and the rest were people of other ethnic groups and those who did not declare themselves as Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Muracevic, is my information that you are a poet correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you could say, amongst other things, that I do write poetry as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that all people are honourable, and particularly poets. And, of course, you also gave your solemn oath here. So may I ask you this: You are not here as an expert of the Bosniak government; you are talking about things that you know reliably. Thank God you know a lot, and, unfortunately, you went through a lot of these things yourself. So because there are so many of these things, why would you also need to look at material that the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina gave you to look at? Were you coached, and who coached you for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the government or anybody else [as interpreted] gave me any kind of documents to prepare myself for this testimony. After 23rd of February, 1996, when we returned to the part of the Serb-controlled Vogosca, I found certain documents in the municipality where I used to work. Among other documents, the documents that we see today here are there. So nobody gave them to me. This is what I found inside the municipal building, in schools, in the Kontiki Bed and Breakfast, in the vicinity of the bunker camp, et cetera. So we are talking about the documents that I personally collected. We are not talking about any documents given to me by the government or anybody else in order to coach me for giving evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you were able to see what happened about 1.000 inhabitants of your village. You couldn't know what happened to about 13.000 people, so let us just confine ourselves to the things that you personally saw or experienced yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us clarify with the transcript again. Did you say, Mr. Muracevic, that government or anybody else gave you any kind of documents to prepare yourself for this testimony? It's line 5 and 6 of page 73.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government did not give me any kind of documents in order to prepare myself. However, the documents that I personally collected were placed at the disposal of various agencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one second, please. I apologise, Mr. Karadzic. Since you asked me and the President took the floor, I failed to give you an answer. In the area of Vogosca municipality, I stayed in the camps until the 5th December 1992. Therefore, I had an opportunity to see and hear what was happening in the area that you controlled in Vogosca, meaning not in my village alone, but in the whole area of Vogosca under the Serbian control. During my detention at various camps, occasionally other people would be brought in, coming from other parts of Vogosca municipality, who then gave me accounts of what was happening in their respective areas. Now, if we talk about the number of people expelled from the territory under your control, this is something that I have personal knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will be grateful to you, and I believe that goes for other participants as well. If you present all of this that you saw yourself, and I'm wondering if what you say -- saw yourself. A minute ago, you gave us a precise number, 13.127, which is the figure that you saw in the papers produced by the Commission for the Investigation of War Crimes. Did you, yourself, acquire this information or did someone provide you with it?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it is not true that these documents were given to me by representatives of the government. That's the document that I personally found in the municipal building in Vogosca, left behind by the Serbs. As for my personal knowledge about the expulsion of the population, I just made a comparison between the two and the document from 1991, and we reached the figure that I mentioned. So I'm talking about the document that was left behind by the Serbs after the 23rd of February, 1996, when this area became an integral part of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that on the premises where the Serbian authorities had been, you found a document produced by a Muslim commission for investigation of war crimes, even before the document was compiled, because it hadn't been compiled before February 1996. Therefore, Mr. Muracevic, I am calling upon you as an honourable poet and man to tell us the truth.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not speaking the truth. I found this document after February 1996 on the premises that prior to that had been controlled by the Serbian side. So nobody gave me that document. I found it personally in the municipal building of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that a document of the Muslim or Bosnian Government or is it a document produced by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document produced by the Serbian authorities, not the Bosnian Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you show us this document?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have the two documents the witness is referring to. I think Mr. Karadzic is confusing the witness somewhat. Mr. Karadzic was given a proofing note the other day which said that there was a Serbian document that was found in the municipal building, and he was also given a document which states in the proofing note that it was authored by the witness, which has the figure of 13.157. So these are the two documents that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That could go on the ELMO, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you like to see that document now, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I know which document is being spoken about by Ms. Sutherland. But the witness spoke about the document produced by the Commission for Investigation of Crimes. This is not the one. That was the kind of interim census that was carried out in the course of the war. I am interested in the document that the witness received from the Commission for Investigation of War Crimes. And if my LiveNote was in order, I would have given you the exact page and line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karadzic, you're not talking truthfully about what we are discussing. I never said that I received this document from the Commission for Investigation of War Crimes. Instead, I found it in the municipal building, upon my arrival on the 23rd of February, 1996, to the territory that had been under the Serb control. Therefore, it is not true that anyone from the Commission for Investigation of Crimes gave me this document, or anyone from the state authorities, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When I asked you how you knew that, didn't you, yourself, mention the Commission for Investigation of Crimes?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I gave you that answer in relation to your public appearance with regard to the plebiscite in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who gave you those documents?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: The ones referring to the plebiscite, is that what you mean, the 1991 plebiscite? Your question is not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who gave you the documents produced by the Commission for Investigation of Crimes that you mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody gave them to me. I said that I read that in a bulletin of that commission, and part of those speeches were published in the media; specifically, in "Oslobodjenje" newspaper, where reference was made to your statements given during the plebiscite. So nobody gave me that personally. I rather had an opportunity to read it in a public document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Witness, you said here that I said in a public speech, which is something that I actually said in a closed meeting of my party, and that was an interpretation of what I had discussed with Mr. Izetbegovic in private. Now, who gave you the documents that were not in the public domain?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: There is no such document. I just quoted part of the speech that you delivered before the 1991 plebiscite. There were broader statements carried in the media, and there were lots of things that you said apart from what I wanted, so in the bulletin of the State Commission for Investigation of Crimes, part of it was published in "Oslobodjenje." Unfortunately, I don't have the copy of that newspaper with me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. What you're talking about now, did you know all of that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew some things, because your fiery speeches at the SDS rally were intended to awaken the national consciousness of Serbs. Perhaps you did not directly instigate certain things, but you used to express yourselves in a poetic way, as you did, and that provoked a certain reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to get an answer from you, because you didn't know anything about what you cited from that meeting because that wasn't published, and you didn't know that in 1992. Are you trying to say that the Serbian peasants knew about that in 1992, or is it that they went to spend the nights in the Serbian villages because they were afraid of what might happen to them?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that members of the Serbian population could have known that, because they regularly attended various rallies and meetings of yours, where you gave a variety of speeches, and that applied to my fellow villagers. I don't know whether they went to this particular meeting that had to do with the preparation for a plebiscite, but they did attend the meetings that you held.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it the time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll have a break for 30 minutes and resume at three minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, in early March you sent your family to Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not send my family to Germany in early March, but rather my family, that is to say, my wife and my children, on the day when our village was attacked, went to pay a visit to my wife's mother. And then from there, during the war, they left for Germany and joined my brother there, who had been working there for quite a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I am now confused, Mr. Muracevic. It says here, in paragraph 2 of your amalgamated statement: [In English] "My wife and children left B and H in March 1992, and returned in 1996, after the war." [Interpretation] And you said a similar thing in one of the interviews that you had with the Prosecution in 1996, immediately before your family returned.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: My family left my village in May 1992. On the 2nd of May, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you then say here that they left in March?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I can't now compare and explain various statements that I made. I don't know why it says "March," but I know that they left the village on the day when the village was attacked, and they went to Visoko to join my wife's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when did they leave Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992. I didn't know exactly. They lived in Visoko with my mother-in-law for a certain period of time, then they moved to my sister's place in Zenica, and then they established contact with my brother in Germany, and eventually they left for Germany in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which month?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time, but I think it was towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you find out when they left?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I spoke with my family for the first time in 1993, after I escaped from the camp. So I spoke to them for the first time on that occasion, and that is when I found out that they were practically living with my brother in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But after your escape, one day after your escape, you told the Muslim authorities that your family was at Visoko?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when I escaped, I knew that they were in Visoko, but I didn't know that they had already left Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that moment when I gave them this statement, I was not aware of the fact that they had left Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is something that I learned only in 1993; that is to say, that they were not living in Bosnia any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But after 1993, you knew when they left. Why did you maintain your claim that they left in March?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: It must have been a misprint. I have always claimed that they left in May, so it's probably a misprint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that you organised night guards to protect the Serbian houses in your village?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Alongside the local police and the population, we made an effort towards protecting these houses from being looted by criminals or preventing any incidents happening that might cause the Serbs to say that their property was under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, Mr. Muracevic. And in spite of the guards and this protection, the Serbs preferred to go to spend nights in other villages. Wasn't everything that you did enough to make them feel safe? I think maybe it was just the contrary. That is what made them go out and sleep elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that you are describing the situation correctly. I even think that Serbs had certain instructions about the attack on our village by the Serbs, even before the 2nd of May, when the village was attacked. Probably due to this kind of information, they decided to leave the village in order to avoid becoming a target of their own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understand that you were thinking, because, as they say, everyone has a back and everyone has a thought in his mind, but, I mean, do not tell us what you think. Tell us what you know.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: They started leaving our village towards the end of 1991. Immediately after the multi-party elections, people felt in my village that inter-ethnic relations were being disrupted. It was particularly due to the influence of the neighbouring village of Krivoglavci, where 215 citizens of Serb ethnicity, in relation to the municipality of Vogosca, where there were representatives of Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats, they sent a petition, actually, to this Vogosca Municipal Assembly to ask for banning the sale of Serb houses to Muslims and to prohibit Muslims from building houses in that village. So all of that, in a way, affected their behaviour in our village. Towards the end, in 1991, they started leaving, and in 1992, it was practically an everyday occurrence. In view of everything that happened at the beginning of May, it probably indicates what -- that they knew what would happen to my village even before the village was actually attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Six months before that?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, precisely in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This petition, did you bring the OTP this petition not to have farms and property sold to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't brought it, but it's a public document. You can find it in the archives of the municipality. I didn't bring that, and I didn't attach it to my documents, but that is a fact, and it can easily be found in the archives of the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Muracevic, if I say that you gave at least 10 statements and other forms of testimony?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it could be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many -- in how many statements and testimonies did you mention that petition?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Several, a few, possibly. I cannot say that with any degree of certainty now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we are going to ask the distinguished Ms. Sutherland to save the day for us, because I have not found that in a single one of your statements or in a single one of the testimonies you provided. This is the first I hear of it. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything for sure. I mean, I know how many statements you have there at your disposal, but I just mentioned this petition. I mean, I didn't attach it here. So it is a fact that at one of the first sessions after the multi-party elections, one of the first sessions of the Municipal Assembly, where the SDS participated as well, this kind of document was received, and that can be found in the municipal archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a first-rate document. If it exists, we certainly need it. If it does not exist, then, Mr. Muracevic, your statement and your testimony that you are providing just now look quite different, don't they?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: The document does exist, and we shall do our best to have it provided to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, in paragraph 8 of your statement, your amalgamated statement, that after the referendum, incidents started occurring, the Public Security Station was split up on an ethnic basis, roadblocks were set up, et cetera. Are you linking these roadblocks to the referendum?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, these barricades/roadblocks have to do with the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sorry, although there were some barricades - perhaps I can call them that - but there were some check-points at the entrance to certain villages that were primarily Serb populated. They existed before, too. But if we're talking about barricades and roadblocks, we basically link them to the period around the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what you said about before the referendum, could you please give us specific information and proof to that effect? But you did mention that these barricades had something to do with developments related to the referendum. What particular developments are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992, there was a referendum that had to do with citizens stating their views on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Already during the night of the 29th of February, things started happening. In Krivoglavci, which is a village near the Vogosca fly-over, there was shooting, so the balloting station had to be closed there. On the 1st of March, 1992, the local population of Serb ethnicity got an enormous quantity of weapons out of the Semizovac Barracks. This was weaponry of the Territorial Defence that was actually stored at the Semizovac Barracks, and all of this was taken to Krivoglavci, Kotorovici, above Semizovac, and other places that were populated by Serbs. After the 2nd of March, the roadblocks cropped up all over town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, are you trying to say that the Serbs were hindering that referendum, obstructing it?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: In Blagovac and other areas, yes. As a matter of fact, the Local Commune of Blagovac did not allow a balloting station to be placed in Blagovac because one of the voting stations had to be moved to the university in Vogosca. And as for Krivoglavci, since the referendum went on for two days, the polling station in Krivoglavci had to be closed down because of the provocations of the Serbs. There was shooting and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, do you know that we received compliments from the United Nations and the European Union because we made it possible for Muslims and Croats to vote? In Serb-populated villages and towns, there weren't balloting stations because the Serbs did not want to vote; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is not right. I don't know about these compliments. But as for the question of voting in Krivoglavci and Blagovac, that could not be linked to those compliments, because the voting was actually obstructed in those places. Also, there were some Serbs who voted at that referendum. Specifically in my Local Commune of Svrake, there were Serbs who came to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And why was this not carried by the press? That is close to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're not telling the truth or you didn't read the local newspapers, especially in relation to these incidents in Krivoglavci, at the polling station there. That was reported in the press. As a matter of fact, during the night between the first and second day of the referendum in Krivoglavci, the Serb population even attacked a police car in which there were three policemen of different ethnic backgrounds. There were even Serbs among them. It was riddled with bullets from rifles, because during the night -- between the first and second night in Krivoglavci, there was some shooting, and in this way pressure was brought to bear on the Adrovic family, and also the next day the police patrol intervened and was attacked by the Serb population -- the local Serb population. This patrol managed to leave through my village. So from Krivoglavci, they escaped to Svrake, and from Svrake, they managed to get to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is this? Is this a unit or is it villagers from Krivoglavci?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say whether it's a unit or whether it's the villagers, but the local population, that most probably had weapons. Well, I didn't really testify about this incident, but I was a witness when this police patrol got out of Krivoglavci and came to Svrake. I personally went with them to the police station in Vogosca in order to get there, because they were so scared by everything that was going on because of this gun-fire that had been opened at them, at policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Why are you and I beating about the bush? Why are we not talking about the main thing that happened; that is to say, the roadblocks? Why are we avoiding that? Is it not true that the barricades were put up because a member of a Serb wedding party was killed near Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about that. I wasn't the organiser of these roadblocks or barricades, so I cannot speak about that. At any rate, it did happen during that period of time. But I cannot testify that that was the reason, the killing of the member of the Serb wedding party there or the referendum, because I had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you cannot say that it was the referendum that was the reason for that? You've just said so.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all of that has to do with these situations. It has to do with this period of time. Now, what the real cause was, you probably know that because you organised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, you say that in addition to these barricades and all of that, the Public Security Station was split up on an ethnic basis; isn't that right? Do you remember that or do you want me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime in March, there was this division of the police force along ethnic lines, so, yes, yes, that it happened, the police station was split up on an ethnic basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Muslims erect roadblocks at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the same time. It was only after -- afterwards, when the Muslim population saw these barricades that were erected by the Serbs. Then for a short period of time, barricades were placed in certain neighbourhoods, but very soon they were removed and no longer existed. After these barricades that were put up in March, Serbs were placing barricades, roadblocks, at check-points, and they continued to check vehicles and people passing there. So they did keep these check-points under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the barricades were not lifted already on the 3rd of March throughout Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, they were lifted by the Serb Democratic Party throughout Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that they were not removed on the 3rd of March, the barricades? What you said about the Serb Democratic Party, you would have to prove that, Mr. Muracevic, and please stick to what you know, please.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: The representatives of Serbs who put up barricades that had to do with the 2nd of March, I mean, the roadblocks, themselves, were removed. But in most places in the municipality of Vogosca where these roadblocks did exist, there were still physical checks that were carried out by representatives of the Serb police and the Serb forces. They were checking vehicles and also the movement of people in and out of various neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what you say in paragraph 8: [In English] "After that, Vogosca Public Security Station employees split up on ethnic basis. Muslim and Croat policemen moved to the village of Svrake and set up a police station and a check-point along the Sarajevo-Zenica main road, in the village of Svrake." [Interpretation] Who placed these check-points, according to paragraph 8 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, part of the local population, part of the police force, and part of the Territorial Defence; right? Well, around us, Serb forces had placed their check-points all over, so this was a way of protecting our neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's Muslims and Croats, as this paragraph says; right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Muslims, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then in that way, the road leading to Zenica was obstructed, or rather one had to pass through that check-point; right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No. The Sarajevo-Zenica road was not stopped in any way. Vehicles of the JNA and all other vehicles could just pass both ways. That is to say that the JNA passed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there such a check-point at Kobilja Glava as well?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I think so. So in response to the barricades erected by the Serbs, counter-check-points were erected in areas where the Muslims were a majority; specifically, Kobilja Glava, Barice, Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are predominantly Muslim neighbourhoods; right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, most of the population was Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 9, you say that: "Serbs held the top positions in the overall system at that time, in terms of military, politics, economy, education, simply everything." You say "simply everything." Do you stand by that assertion?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I do. In my municipality, in all key positions, regardless of whether it had to do with the municipality, the police, schools, any other public institutions, even the barracks in Semizovci, it was the Serbs who held all of these top positions. I can also testify to that because I was secretary of the Municipal Conference of the Socialist Alliance of the Working People at the time just before the referendum or, rather, the multi-party elections in 1990, and I, therefore, had an opportunity of seeing this; that is to say, what the personnel situation was in the municipality of Vogosca. Just before the multi-party elections, when the term of office would expire of, say, the president of the municipality, or the head of the League of Communists in the municipality, or the principals of various schools, and so on and so forth, instead of agreeing on what the ethnic structure would be, in accordance with the number of inhabitants from different ethnic groups, most of these office-holders had their terms extended. So there was no ethnic balance in these top positions. It was primarily Serbs who remained in all these positions of top authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, is the municipality of Vogosca an integral part of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, yes, it was an integral part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that in the town of Sarajevo in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb national community was dominant, holding all the levers of power?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Based on what I could see in my municipality and in all other parts, mostly, all the significant posts, for the most part, were held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know who Alija Delimustafic was?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim, and was he a member -- a minister of internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Muslim and minister of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was Avdo Hebib a Muslim, and was he his police deputy?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, you want me to testify about the structure of the town, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was subjected to certain torture in the municipality of Vogosca, primarily in the settlement of Svrake, so I would like to speak about those positions. When I said in my statement that all the key positions were held by Serbs, what I mainly meant was the municipality of Vogosca and in the territory where I lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was the president of the municipality in Vogosca a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, the president of the municipality, after God knows how many years, was finally a Muslim. I can count on the fingers of one hand the number of Muslims who were appointed to such high-ranking positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the chief of the Public Security Station and the number-one person in Internal Affairs; was that a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: At one point, it was. But as soon as the multi-party elections were held, then again the post went to a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Vehid Hodzic; is he a Serb?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, Vehid Hodzic was one of the Muslims who was appointed at the head of the police. Before that, no Muslim was at the head of a police station. After the multi-party elections -- after the multi-ethnic elections in 1990, there was a kind of balancing carried out to a degree to have the president of the municipality post given to a Muslim. The police head was given to a Muslim. I was also talking about the situation before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But at the time when the crisis erupted in Vogosca, which is what we're talking about, are you saying that the Serbs held all the main levers of power in the municipality of Vogosca, in the city of Sarajevo, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina? But let's stand -- let's stay with Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Vogosca municipality who presided over the legislative body where half of the membership was Muslim, but the head of the Executive Board was a Muslim, and that is practically the executive power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, do you remember that only as of recently the executive authority became more important, but at that time the number-one person would be the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that may sound like that, but executive power, after all, is executive power. The president of the municipality, at least as far as this first person who was elected after the multi-party elections, was not really asked about much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We will come to this in more detail later. You are probably familiar with the directives -- I will wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure if there's -- the witness has misspoken or -- it's page 92, lines 2, 3, and 4, when he was saying who the president of the Vogosca municipality was, and then who was the head of the executive board, what ethnicities they were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard that from previous witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But perhaps we can confirm that, that the president of the municipality was a Muslim and the president of the Executive Board was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in that system, was the president of the municipality superior to the president of the Executive Board; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: In a way, the president of the Executive Board was not above the president of the municipality, but practically it was the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Practically, the Muslim president of the municipality was a superior to the president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the way the situation was at the time, the Executive Board was taken much more into account. The president of the municipality was the one who would convene all the different positions and ask people to do what was needed, but the Executive Board president already had his own body, and within that body they could implement certain decisions without needing to resort to any outside bodies. As soon as that body was convened, the president of the Executive Board could implement decisions until the next Assembly was convened or until somebody drew his attention to the fact that perhaps he wasn't doing his job properly. But on paper, the president of the municipality was the number-one post and a superior in relation to the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the Executive Board? Was the Executive Board president able to act outside of the Secretariat or did they act under the auspices of the Secretariat, and did his cabinet consist of a secretary?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot go into the composition of the actual cabinet, but the president of the Executive Board was asked about everything. I don't know if he consulted with members of his cabinet. I'm thinking about other members of the Secretariat. This not something that I can talk much about, because I'm not really that knowledgeable about the details, how the meetings were conducted and how he executed his duties as the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, you were a president -- you were a part of the system. You were the secretary of the Local Commune. Is it correct that the municipal government comprises the Secretariat and that the cabinet is comprised of secretaries; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, that's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the main secretarial functions in the Executive Board of Vogosca were held by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Look, my previous statement, which talks about the relationships which preceded all of this that happened, what I spoke about what, up to 1990, was the situation up to the multi-party elections, when all key functions were held by Serbs, this is what I talked about. After the multi-party elections, there was a certain balance achieved in the execution of these functions, but practically this was not something that functioned. It didn't function properly, because representatives of the Executive Board, Serbs mostly, reached agreement with the president of the Executive Board, and those members did not, in turn, consult much with the members of the Executive Board who were Muslims. Mostly, they implemented the positions that they felt should be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you didn't attend those meetings, and that is your impression?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my impression. So I didn't really want to go into a debate about the work of that government, but the impression was that mostly representatives in the Executive Board who were Serbs consulted more with the president of the Executive Board and implemented those positions they saw fit, and to a lesser degree did they consult with members of the Executive Board who were from the Muslim ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we're dealing with the Executive Board now, but you don't know that. You didn't attend the meeting, so you don't know that. Do you know that the main Secretariats were in the hands of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is what I'm telling you: The policies implemented by the Executive Board did not correspond to what was established at meetings of the Municipal Assembly, and what should have been established and ascertained at the meetings of the Executive Board. It actually took a completely different course that was to the advantage of the Serbs, in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, earlier on you said that the president of the Executive Board cannot act in any other way other than through the Secretariat, so how do you explain this impression of yours that something was done when the president of the Executive Board does not have the power, other than what is implied in the power of the secretariats or the secretaries?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain what that means. In a certain period, my local commune, in order to implement a specific project, should have received 200.000 dinars at the time. I don't know the value. And then, at the proposal of the Executive Board, it was said that only 100.000 dinars was awarded in order to implement that project. So now there is the question: If it was agreed that it would be given 200.000 dinars, why did the president of the government then only give us 100.000? So based on things like this, one would gain the impression that the president of the Executive Board did not care much for the opinion of his colleagues in the Executive Board who happened to be Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Muracevic. By that analogy, in each government in Europe, the Serbs would be in charge, because all governments function like that; they promise you something, and then they give you a half of it. But, anyway, is it true that the war began in your area on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: The attack was carried out or began on the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you in your statement you said that: "The war in our area began on the 2nd of May." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For me specifically and for my Local Commune, it began on the 2nd of May, although the given is that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina began a bit earlier, didn't it? Already, shells were falling before the 2nd of May, launched by Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just leave aside the things that you don't know. We have a list of the expended ammunition daily, as it pertains to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: It's not that I didn't know that shells were falling on Sarajevo. You could hear detonations in Vogosca as well. The detonations of shells dropping on Sarajevo could be heard in Vogosca and also in the place where I was living; namely, Svrake. So you cannot say that I didn't know that shells were hitting Sarajevo before the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So how do you explain that from the 6th of April, when war broke out in Sarajevo, until the 2nd of May, there was no war where you were?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: How do I think that possible? My village, before the 2nd of May, was completely encircled. From the beginning of 1992, it was literally encircled by Serbian forces that were around the village, and that they had armed guards, trenches. And then from the March barricades on, literally, the village found it difficult to bring in food into the shops that were still working. Very often, citizens were inspected at these check-points. At some check-points, even cars were confiscated from our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In another place, Mr. Muracevic, you said that events further away from Svrake were responsible for the shortages of food, and it's not the way you are telling it today.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not true that I said that it had to do with events farther than Svrake. From the beginning, from 1992, my village was completely blocked by Serbian forces, which literally monitored the entrance of each individual, and each individual village [as interpreted], that entered the settlement, including the supply vehicles. So from the beginning of 1992 until the attack on my village, the shops had a lot of difficulty to obtain food articles in order for the people to be able to buy them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, in paragraph 8 earlier, we read that the check-points near your village were held by Muslims, not Serbs, so now this is something new. Nobody knew about this before now. What encirclement? Which forces encircled the village of Svrake from the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't know whether you are deliberately or unintentionally twisting everything that I'm saying. If you look at my village, Svrake, on the map it was strategically surrounded by places that were controlled by the Serbian population. All key directions, Vogosca, Semizovac, Ilijas, the Zenica-Sarajevo motorway that could provide entries into my area, were -- had check-points at the entrance of my village of Svrake, at Manjez, from the direction of Ilijas. There was also a check-point controlled by the Serbs. Also at the Vogosca roundabout leading from the motorway. The Muslim police in Svrake, you could say, didn't -- I apologise -- didn't have many check-points. Beyond the Muslim check-points, there were check-points by Serb policemen from the direction of Ilijas, from the direction of Vogosca, because the motorway passes through Svrake. So from the direction of Ilijas, before you entered Svrake, in a part of the village called Malacici [phoen], there was a Serbian check-point, as well as on the point where you exit from Svrake and you go towards Krivoglavci, going towards the Vogosca motorway. These were the points where the Serbs had set up their check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, let us save on time a little bit. Am I correct if I were to say that earlier you said that Svrake was encircled by Serbian forces, and then after that, just now, you say that Svrake was encircled by Serbian settlements? Which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Both are true, both encircled by Serbian forces and encircled by Serbian settlements. Krivoglavci, Ilijas, were settlements that were under the control of the Serbs. The entire area around my village, Svrake, meaning Krivoglavci, Paljevo, Semizovac, were held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were Serbs living there or were some armed forces there?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Both. There were people living there and there were armed forces there, and they did this alongside the Serbian police forces deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before 27th of March, 1992, was there a Serbian police force?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Even before the division of the police along the ethnic lines in March, it operated before 1992 as two component organisations. They were all together in the same police station, but they did not act exactly together. However, I am reluctant to talk much about the police work, because I have no knowledge about how these structures functioned. All I know is that it often happens that the Serb policemen assisted the barricades, that they were checking mainly Muslims and Croats, which created an impression that even before they were officially divided along ethnic lines, they acted separately as two components.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Muslim police officers man the check-points?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: If we talk about the Vogosca junction, the main roads connecting Semizovac, and further on with Tuzla, Zenica, Sarajevo, were mainly manned by the Serbian police officers. Maybe a Muslim or two was with them at times, but I never saw any of them at these check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the check-points on the motorway to Zenica, in the area of Svrake, were those held by ordinary people or by the police?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Mainly by ordinary people and by reserve police force. Some of the Muslim officers that were present there were more involved in maintaining law and order inside the village, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, I'm not holding you responsible for these check-points, but you said precisely in paragraph 8 that those things were done by the policemen?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. When I say "police," I meant the reserve police force, because in a certain manner, they acted as one single component.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Hasan Efendic, the commander of the BH Territorial Defence, had issued two directives to attack the JNA and the Serbs? One of them was dated the 12th of April, and the other one was dated the 29th of April.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you know what happened at Pretis on the night between the 17th and the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less, I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we take a look for a moment at D400.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this second directive that was issued towards the end of April?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about either the first one or the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, do you accept that the 29th of April is a date very close to the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't need me to confirm that. It is so obvious from these two dates that they are not far apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this directive, please. Does it say: "I order full and massive blockade along all the road intersections on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on which the units of the former JNA are beginning to withdraw technical and material assets along with the MUP. "Carry out the blockade of the wider region of military objects ...," et cetera. Did you have any military facilities in Svrake?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any military facilities in Svrake. Now, first of all, speaking about this document, I must say that this is the first time that I'm seeing it, and I absolutely had no knowledge of it in 1992. As I said, this is the first time that I am seeing it. As I said, there were no military facilities in the village of Svrake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was this military facility, and how far your house was from it?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA barracks in Semizovac was on the right-hand bank of the River Bosna, and my house was on the left-hand-side bank of the Bosna River, exactly opposite the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this item 2, which says: "Carry out the blockade of the wider region of military facilities ..." Did this include this military facility that you mentioned, regardless of the fact that you didn't know how and on the basis of what the developments took place?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the barracks is concerned, it is a military facility. But I can't tell you what the intention of the author of this order is. I know that there was no attack launched from Svrake against this military facility, in relation to this order or any other order, for that matter. This military facility was situated in a different local commune on the other bank of the River Bosna, and all the main roads at the time were under the Serbian control. Therefore, there was no possibility for anyone to threaten this kind of facility, and we didn't have any resources to do that anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have 1D3354.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You managed to escape on the 5th of December; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You gave your first statement on the 6th of December, which means one day after you escaped?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Somewhere in the middle, after the paragraph which begins: "The 1st of March ... ," it says that: "Military columns started moving in all directions, due to which, because of the directive not to touch the army, and due to the lack of proper materiel and equipment, we did not stop these convoys or control them." So it means that you knew that there were directives, and then among them was the directive not to touch the army?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a publicly-known thing. The Muslim leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina called upon the people to refrain from entering into clashes with the JNA. There was no written directive to that effect. It just arrived from various statements given by politicians for the people not to clash with the JNA. The fact is that columns were passing through my village and through Semizovac, made up of the JNA assets obviously stationed in the Serb-controlled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that on the 23rd or the 24th of December, the military leadership of Yugoslavia came and held a meeting with the entire leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in which the Muslim part of the leadership wanted the JNA to be more proactive and active in preventing inter-ethnic conflicts? Was that something that was published?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember the details. I know that there were various alternatives relating to how the JNA should not interfere and how they could help the people, but I can't recall exactly all the details. I know that there were various options on the table for the JNA to become more actively involved in trying to calm down conflicts, but we were all witnesses of how that happened and that it did not happen exactly as how you had agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take part in military defence preparations in your village?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a certain way, after having studied everything that was happening around us, we were, in a sort of way, forced to protect ourselves in the event of a possible attack on our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were an active participant in the defence preparations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way, but I was not solely responsible for that. But you can say that as the secretary of the Local Commune, in a way, it was my responsibility and duty to take care of the population living in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this paragraph, please, which is second from the bottom, which reads: "On the 1st of May, I, Ferid Cutura, commander of the Svrake Territorial Defence, Nijaz Salkic, an active policeman, in agreement with Mirsad Durak, a Gras driver who often parked his bus in front of my house in Svrake, decide to transfer one mortar in a Gras bus to Grad, to the Police Officers' Club, which we succeeded in doing, even though we had to pass through two of their barricades. On our way back from town ..." Now, let's stop here. Do you know that as early as on the 6th of April, separation lines were established, but you managed to cross them with this mortar?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, speaking about this mortar, one needs to know that the barricade that was erected on the motorway stopped a vehicle driven by a Serb. Having inspected the vehicle, they established that certain parts of materiel mentioned here were in that car. Since we did not need those pieces of equipment and materiel in Svrake, and we had no intention of using them, we decided to transfer them to the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the way described in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's forget about this car driven by a Serb. In Svrake, you had a mortar, and your judgement was that it could be put to a better use in the city of Sarajevo. So you loaded it onto a Gras bus, you crossed the separation line, you passed through the Serbian check-point, and you managed to deliver it in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you a simple answer as it is correct or not correct. We are speaking about some of the equipment and materiel that in the days before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you why you did it. I'm asking you if you did it.

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: You can see, from the minutes, what I did. But the circumstances that brought this about had to do with the fact that the local Serbs were receiving weapons from the JNA barracks, and the mortar, driven by a Serb, was confiscated on the road. Since we did not have any intention of firing at Serbs from mortars, we decided to pass it on to the legal formation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which at the time was the Territorial Defence of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not need it, because we didn't want to fight anyone by using a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you confiscate this mortar from this Serb?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: That was on the night before the 1st of May, which means the last day of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you provide a description of that?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, I didn't provide a description? What do you mean by that, if you see that I described this event in all the statements I gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, how did you manage to pass through -- over the front-line? At that time, a public city bus was able to cross over?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, if a public bus set off from Sarajevo, it could only pass through the territory controlled by the Serbs. If it went from Kobilja Glava to Donja Vogosca, which is on the other end of Vogosca, when it turned back, the whole time it had to pass through the barricades controlled by the local Serbs. So in that respect, the transport was done in that way, because we made use of a bus that had been in Svrake, and it managed to pass through Vogosca and onwards to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What would have happened if you had been detected and discovered by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would probably have shot us dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here: "Upon return from the town, and after consultation with the TO Municipal Staff, Bakir Alispahic, Vehbija Karic and Mustafa Hajrulahovic, it was agreed that we transfer the mortars to Sarajevo." "Ferid Cutura and I, in a Jetta police car, took mortar shells, and we hid it within the food articles that we were transferring and transporting for the police." Now, it seems that you were brave and you managed to hide four mortars intended for Svrake, which means that it's not true that you had no intention of opening fire from Svrake?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did not intend to go to Sarajevo. However, the circumstances prevailing at the time couldn't guarantee anything. And I think that it would have been impossible for us to repeat what we did on the 1st of May, which is to say to transfer the mortars to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbs aware of these activities that you were carrying out?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I assume they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic misstates the record. It's actually one mortar and four rounds for a mortar, not four mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is a wrong translation, although I do not hold it against them, because due to such speed that we speak at, they might make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muracevic, were you a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: By virtue of my position as the secretary of the Local Commune, I was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Svrake local community?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my local commune, and I co-ordinated things in a certain way with the Vogosca Crisis Staff. I'm referring to the part where the Muslims were a majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was the Svrake Crisis Staff formed?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections and when all those things started happening, there was an attempt, together with the local residents, to rally people more, and it all started towards the end of September or early October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the municipal Crisis Staff established at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was also established sometime in mid-September or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me jog your memory now. Can we have the first page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph says: "Up until the moment when taken prisoner ..." Mr. Muracevic, do you distinguish between taken prisoner and arrests?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, arrests and prisoner-taking, it's one-and-the-same thing for me. I mean, arrests, well, it means I'm taken prisoner when the population is leaving our village; that is to say, on the 4th of May, 1992. That is to say, together with a column of people from Svrake. When, in agreement with the representatives of the local Serbs in Semizovac, when it was agreed upon that they would let the citizens of Svrake leave through Semizovac, I was in that column. However, the Serbs did not honour that agreement, and they let part of the column pass, and they took prisoner or arrested another part of the column, this group that was taken to the Semizovac Barracks. And I was included in that group, so that was when I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I continue with this paragraph: Is it true that after this confusion, it's the fault of your two Muslim negotiators who did not inform you what the Serbs had promised them; rather, they just got their own people out, and you just managed to show up there without any agreement having been reached with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, our negotiators told people that at 2.00, they would stop firing at us, and that during that interval, whoever wanted to leave the village could. However, the area of my local commune is rather big. Not all the people from my local commune were in a single building. They were throughout the territory of the Local Commune. So over this short period of time, it was not possible to get almost 1.000 people to gather there so that they could pass through this -- or, rather, by this barricade over an hour or two. The Serbs said that they would allow two hours for this passage, but already after an hour, an hour and twenty minutes, they did not -- they cut the column and did not allow all the people from Svrake to get to Breza and other parts of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to that. In one statement, Mr. Muracevic, you said that your negotiators kept some information from you, what kind of guarantees they got from the Serbs. They took their own people, and when they left, the people organised themselves, and then that column was stopped; is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, I cannot give a mere yes-or-no answer to your question. When the negotiators returned, they explained what the terms were. However, the problem is the following: As I and some of my co-workers were walking all over the village, trying to rally all the people to gather, these negotiators managed to leave the village first of all, and those who lived closest to the highway between Zenica and Sarajevo left together with them, and also some others who were there simply didn't have enough time to leave with them. That is where this thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this explanation, the agreed column passed and the non-agreed column was stopped?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The agreement reached was that the entire village could leave. However, the Serbs did not honour that agreement. So as the column was leaving the village, they simply cut it off. Those who managed to get through did, and the rest were taken to the barracks in Semizovac. I was in this second group. As the secretary of the Local Commune who had worked there for 10 years, I could not allow myself to be at the head of the column and to be the first to leave, whereas some of my citizens would be left behind. I tried to be among the last people who would be leaving the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My apologies, Ms. Sutherland. I kept you standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Karadzic can give me the statement that he's referring to, I'd be very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I will certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up until the moment when you were taken prisoner, do you agree that a criminal is arrested, but a fighter, an honest man, is taken prisoner, so you did not explain it properly here?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I explained specifically what it meant to be taken prisoner. They simply cut off the column. I was with this group of people who remained in the village, and I was taken to the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, and that, in a way, was one of the first camps that were established for the inhabitants of my municipality, or, rather, my local commune.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm worried about whether "taken prisoner" is a proper translation. I would like to have the word "capturing" used.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Taken captive."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, let me continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I was not involved in the Territorial Defence. I was a member of the Crisis Staff when it was headed by Abdil Kula and later by Murat Cutura." Let us stop at this point. This Murat Cutura, was he in the police of Vogosca? Was he some important person up there?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he did work in the Vogosca police. Now, I don't know whether he was a really important person. He did work at the police station in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that Skrbic, Zoran Skrbic or whatever his name was, was dismissed, and this Murat Cutura replaced him at the police station?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. But Murat Cutura was one of the officers at the police station, and, in a way, he did something there. He issued permits for weapons or whatever. I wasn't really that familiar with the structure of the police station, itself, and I didn't know what was actually going on within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that the transcript misstates that you were not involved in the Territorial Defence. You said that you were involved in the Territorial Defence, and in your statement you say: "I was involved in the organisation of the Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, as secretary of the Local Commune, it is only logical that I was involved in all of this that had to do with the life and work of my local commune, and that included protection from everything that was going on around us and what started happening around our village months before that, and there was this danger or threat that a certain conflict could happen and my village would be attacked too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. "At the same time, I was a member of the Crisis Staff for Svrake, Semizovac, and Gora. Through an organised group of five youths, we were in contact with the Green Berets, the radio station we had was operated by Dzafer Devic from Svrake. Given that the Territorial Defence units had been disbanded earlier, we were working on manning the police reserve formation and later on recruiting people into the new TO unit. In co-operation with the municipal Crisis Staff, I was engaged in the acquisition of weapons for the settlements of Svrake, Semizovac, and Gora, which we were paying between 600 and 800 German marks apiece, depending on the type of barrels. Certain SDA activists were involved in the acquisition of weapons through their channels too." Did the Serbs know what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course they did, because they were the main sellers of this weaponry, because people from my local commune and the neighbouring local commune, days before these activities, entered the army barracks in Semizovac and, quite literally, got all these weapons free of charge. Later on, they sold them to the persons you mentioned there. At any rate, it wasn't that this was some kind of organised procurement of weaponry. Basically, it meant buying weapons from the local Serbs who got these weapons from the soldiers of the JNA from the Semizovac Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Murat Cutura and Ferid Cutura, are they related?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know whether they are related. However -- well, I don't know whether they are related.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's an unusual surname. Are you not aware of the fact that they are closely related; that they're brothers, as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I don't know about that, and I really wouldn't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Muracevic, can you explain to all of us here why your amalgamated statement does not contain any of this from the first two pages of this statement?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as secretary of the Local Commune, I dealt with the organisation of life and work in the territory of the municipality -- or, rather, the Local Commune, and that includes the protection of the local population. It meant that everything was included. In the statement that was handed over here, there is a reference to statements as documents. I don't see how this could have been concealed from you in any way. I mean, the statement that I gave, and that is subject of this other statement, too, I mean, there is a reference to these other statements that you are quoting just now, so I don't think that anything has been concealed. After all, there is nothing to hide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness is right when he says in the amalgamated witness statement, at paragraph 11, it talks about the organisation and what the witness was doing in relation to the TO and the weapons, and it actually footnotes and gives the B/C/S page as well as the English page, to assist Mr. Karadzic. So this earlier statement is actually footnoted in paragraph 11, when the witness describes all of what Mr. Karadzic just talked about, except for the price of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But this buying and selling of weapons does not actually fit into Mr. Muracevic's assertions made in his subsequent statements, that Svrake was not armed and that they had only hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Isn't that right? That's what you said in your subsequent statements, that Svrake did not have enough weapons and that the only weapons that the people there had were hunting weapons?

utterances.speaker: ESET MURACEVIC
utterances.text: All the weapons that existed there were so few, in relation to what had been pointed at us. People who bought some weapons there at very high prices, without the right kind of ammunition, I mean, that really didn't mean very much for the defence of our village, because, basically, people paid money for weapons for which you could not find ammunition in the market for years even before that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
